nh-cmc-granite-united-way-family-first-r.text: catholic medical center grant expands manchester family and first-responder support a $25,000 grant to granite united way will fund school resources, infant-safety supplies and mental-health training for first responders. catholic medical center has awarded granite united way a $25,000 grant aimed at supporting manchester children, new mothers and first responders through several community programs. the hospital said the funding will help provide back-to-school resources and supplies, infant-safety education and kits for new mothers and babies. it also will support mental-health training designed for emergency personnel who routinely encounter traumatic events. according to the hospital, the grant will fund multiple day-long training sessions for nearly 100 first responders and expand outreach intended to reach more than 100 families. the award is part of a broader $2 million community commitment by cmc parent hca healthcare. the projects address different needs but share an early-intervention focus: giving families practical supplies at vulnerable moments and helping responders recognize and manage the strain of emergency work. because the announcement describes planned services, the next useful measures will be participation, delivery of the promised resources and whether the programs continue after this grant period. new-hampshire new-hampshire new hampshire nh manchester manchester, new hampshire catholic medical center granite united way manchester community health

nh-colby-sawyer-keene-state-field-hockey.excerpt: Abby Olden scored with 20 seconds left before halftime, and the Chargers survived a fourth-quarter push by the Owls.
nh-colby-sawyer-keene-state-field-hockey.text: late first-half goal lifts colby-sawyer past keene state, 3-2 abby olden scored with 20 seconds left before halftime, and the chargers survived a fourth-quarter push by the owls. colby-sawyer handed keene state its first loss of the field-hockey season saturday, winning 3-2 in new london on abby olden’s goal with 20 seconds left in the first half. the chargers improved to 4-0, while the owls fell to 4-1 after twice answering an earlier colby-sawyer lead. brooke farquhar scored twice for the chargers. keene state responded through henley gilstrap and lilah carr, making it 2-2 before olden converted from a penalty corner just before the break. the second half produced no goals, though the owls generated sustained pressure late and forced goalkeeper sophie krauss into several important saves. keene state finished with a 15-12 edge in shots and a 14-7 advantage in penalty corners, including nine shots and seven corners in the fourth quarter. krauss made six saves for colby-sawyer. gilstrap’s goal was her team-leading seventh in five games. the owls return home wednesday to face western new england. new-hampshire new-hampshire new hampshire new hampshire new london new london, new hampshire keene state colby-sawyer field hockey new london

nh-colleges-economic-impact-enrollment-s.excerpt: A new statewide assessment puts higher education's economic impact at $17.1 billion while highlighting sharply different enrollment trends across campuses.
nh-colleges-economic-impact-enrollment-s.text: new hampshire colleges report $17.1 billion impact amid enrollment shifts a new statewide assessment puts higher education's economic impact at $17.1 billion while highlighting sharply different enrollment trends across campuses. new hampshire colleges and universities generated an estimated $17.1 billion in statewide economic activity and supported 114,262 jobs, according to a 2025 report from the new hampshire college and university council cited by the concord monitor. the report also attributed $636 million in state and local tax revenue to the higher-education sector. the statewide picture spans 22 institutions serving more than 320,000 students, including online enrollment, with roughly 66,000 students based in new hampshire. enrollment is not moving evenly. the university of new hampshire reported 2,471 first-year deposits for its incoming class, nearly 4% above last year, while out-of-state deposits rose 7% and in-state deposits remained steady. smaller campuses continue to face pressure. keene state college enrollment has declined from about 5,000 students in 2015 to roughly 2,800 this year, and the school is addressing a $3.3 million deficit with staffing reductions. new hampshire also ranks last nationally in public higher-education funding, while the current state budget reduces four-year public-campus support by 14%. community-college early-college programs now serve more than 11,000 students annually and receive $3 million in state support. new-hampshire new-hampshire new hampshire nh concord new hampshire higher education unh keene state college enrollment new hampshire

nh-colson-whitehead-cool-machine-concord.excerpt: NHPR released an Authors on Main conversation about “Cool Machine,” the third and final book in Whitehead’s Harlem trilogy.
nh-colson-whitehead-cool-machine-concord.text: colson whitehead discusses final harlem novel in concord program nhpr released an authors on main conversation about “cool machine,” the third and final book in whitehead’s harlem trilogy. new hampshire public radio has released a concord conversation with two-time pulitzer prize-winning author colson whitehead focused on “cool machine,” the third and final novel in his harlem trilogy. the installment returns to ray carney, the series’ salesman by day and fence by night, while using his story to examine a changing new york city. nhpr said the discussion explored the novel’s questions about morality, ownership and whether theft committed in response to injustice can be judged in simple terms. the interview was recorded july 24 at the capitol center for the arts as part of nhpr’s authors on main series. julia barnett and olivia comolli presented the program, which was published wednesday as an audio conversation for listeners across new hampshire. the release gives granite state readers a regional entry point into the conclusion of whitehead’s multigenerational crime saga. authors on main brings writers to concord for public discussions, while nhpr books airs saturdays and distributes its conversations through major podcast platforms. the station also maintains an archive of earlier literary interviews and coverage. new-hampshire new-hampshire new hampshire nh concord concord, nh colson whitehead concord cool machine nhpr books

nh-concord-camp-fire-fuel-spill-i93-cras.excerpt: Firefighters, police and state troopers handled several overlapping Thursday-afternoon calls, including a gasoline spill and a two-vehicle interstate crash.
nh-concord-camp-fire-fuel-spill-i93-cras.text: concord crews juggle camp fire, fuel spill and i-93 crash firefighters, police and state troopers handled several overlapping thursday-afternoon calls, including a gasoline spill and a two-vehicle interstate crash. concord public-safety crews responded to a cluster of unrelated incidents thursday afternoon, stretching resources across the city and nearby highways. around 2:15 p.m., smoke reported near interstate 393’s exit 1 led state police to a campsite where people were burning trash. authorities addressed the fire without reporting injuries. minutes later, a truck towing a camper lost its fuel pump near intervale and fort eddy roads. an estimated 25 to 30 gallons of gasoline spilled, requiring firefighters and other crews to contain and clean the scene. the location sits near a busy commercial area and highway approaches, making traffic control part of the response. emergency personnel also went to a two-vehicle crash near interstate 93’s exit 14 involving a toyota driven by a chichester resident and a nissan driven by an antrim resident. no injuries were apparent, but both vehicles needed towing. additional alarm calls followed later in the afternoon. the sequence illustrates how routine incidents can overlap quickly, requiring coordination among city firefighters, concord police and new hampshire state police. new-hampshire new-hampshire new hampshire nh concord concord, new hampshire concord public safety i-93 fuel spill fire

nh-concord-city-manager-tom-aspell-retir.excerpt: The longtime city manager will step down January 31 after 21 years in the role and more than 28 years at City Hall.
nh-concord-city-manager-tom-aspell-retir.text: concord city manager tom aspell to retire in january the longtime city manager will step down january 31 after 21 years in the role and more than 28 years at city hall. concord city manager tom aspell plans to retire january 31, ending more than two decades in the city’s top administrative job and just over 28 years at city hall. aspell announced the decision tuesday after returning from a six-week sabbatical, the concord monitor reported. he became interim city manager in 2005 and received the permanent appointment in 2006, after earlier roles in planning, economic development and as assistant city manager. the retirement starts a significant leadership transition for new hampshire’s capital. concord is also dealing with a deputy city manager vacancy, leaving the city council to decide how to structure and conduct a search while maintaining daily municipal operations. aspell arrived in concord in 1998 after planning and economic-development work in londonderry and haverhill, massachusetts. his january departure gives the council several months to outline a succession process. the city had not yet announced a permanent replacement or a detailed timetable for selecting one. new-hampshire new-hampshire new hampshire nh concord concord, new hampshire concord tom aspell city government retirement

nh-concord-farm-local-greens-2026.excerpt: A two-person farm says it has been selling out weekly as shoppers and restaurants put a premium on local lettuce and microgreens.
nh-concord-farm-local-greens-2026.text: concord farm meets high local demand for greens after lettuce recalls a two-person farm says it has been selling out weekly as shoppers and restaurants put a premium on local lettuce and microgreens. generation farm in concord has been selling out of greens each week this summer, according to new hampshire public radio, as local growers respond to strong demand from restaurants, co-ops and other buyers. james and marley stever run the farm themselves, growing lettuce in outdoor beds and microgreens inside a barn with grow lights. the small operation is handling production, customer service and deliveries with no larger staff behind it. the farm’s busy season comes after cyclospora-related lettuce recalls, including a recall affecting new hampshire, pushed some consumers to reconsider where their produce comes from. the experience shows how a food-safety concern can quickly reshape demand for nearby farms. local farms cannot replace every large-volume supplier, but the concord example shows why direct relationships matter. restaurants and shoppers get a clearer connection to the source, while growers gain a chance to turn a short-term concern into lasting demand for regional food. new-hampshire new-hampshire new hampshire nh concord concord, nh new hampshire concord farming food safety local food

nh-concord-football-alvirne-37-7-2026.excerpt: The Crimson Tide recorded 15 tackles for loss and six sacks before pulling away with two touchdowns and a safety in the third quarter.
nh-concord-football-alvirne-37-7-2026.text: concord defense powers 37-7 win over alvirne the crimson tide recorded 15 tackles for loss and six sacks before pulling away with two touchdowns and a safety in the third quarter. concord high’s defense controlled friday night’s game in hudson, helping the crimson tide defeat alvirne 37-7. the game remained scoreless until the final 34 seconds of the first half, but concord broke it open after halftime with two touchdowns and a safety in the third quarter. the crimson tide finished with 15 tackles for loss, six sacks and a fumble recovery. jax diachenko led the pressure with 3.5 sacks, three tackles for loss and the safety. sebastian telus added five tackles for loss and two sacks, while michael gamache contributed three tackles for loss and a half-sack. dustin ellis forced and recovered a fumble. on offense, colin savard carried 21 times for 176 yards. quarterback rhys craigue completed eight of 19 passes for 142 yards, including an 11-yard touchdown to methuselah doe. a 50-yard gain by savard on a short reception helped set up that score. concord’s combination of backfield disruption and a steady rushing attack turned a tight first half into a decisive road victory. new-hampshire new-hampshire new hampshire new hampshire hudson hudson, new hampshire concord alvirne football high school sports

nh-concord-housing-sensor-privacy-lawsui.excerpt: The ACLU of New Hampshire and New Hampshire Legal Assistance are challenging monitoring devices installed inside subsidized apartments.
nh-concord-housing-sensor-privacy-lawsui.text: concord public-housing sensors face privacy lawsuit the aclu of new hampshire and new hampshire legal assistance are challenging monitoring devices installed inside subsidized apartments. the concord housing and redevelopment authority is facing a lawsuit over electronic monitoring devices installed inside tenants’ apartments. the case was filed in merrimack county superior court by the aclu of new hampshire and new hampshire legal assistance, according to reporting shared by the concord monitor and manchester ink link. the complaint alleges that minut-branded sensors collect information beyond smoke, noise and humidity readings. it says the devices can detect nearby apple devices and motion, creating data that could reveal occupancy patterns. the plaintiffs are asking the court to require deletion of collected data and block lease penalties tied to the monitors while the case proceeds. the housing authority disputes the surveillance allegations. its executive director said the equipment is used for health, safety and property-compliance purposes, does not record audio or video, and has not led to fines or evictions. the authority also said it does not use crowd-monitoring capabilities. the dispute puts emerging property-management technology against expectations of privacy inside a home, particularly for residents receiving public housing assistance. the court has not ruled on the plaintiffs’ claims, and the allegations remain contested. new-hampshire new-hampshire new hampshire nh concord concord, nh concord public housing privacy lawsuit

nh-concord-legislative-garage-sky-glow-2.excerpt: Upward-facing exterior lights on the new legislative parking garage reflected off low clouds, creating a bright patch above downtown.
nh-concord-legislative-garage-sky-glow-2.text: concord garage lights cast glowing rectangle into night sky upward-facing exterior lights on the new legislative parking garage reflected off low clouds, creating a bright patch above downtown. a bright rectangular glow seen over downtown concord came from exterior lights on the new hampshire legislature’s new parking garage reflecting off low clouds, according to the concord monitor. the unusual patch of light appeared above the state house area on cloudy nights and drew questions from residents. the garage, built between the state house and city hall, opened about three weeks ago after replacing the former storrs street parking facility. terry pfaff, chief operating officer of the new hampshire general court, told the monitor that the reflected-light effect was not anticipated during the project. pfaff said the general court would consider reducing the intensity of the lights later at night. that could lessen the glow while preserving illumination around the garage for drivers and pedestrians. because the garage is state-owned, it was not subject to concord planning board review. new hampshire’s dark sky policy discourages upward-directed outdoor lighting, making the episode a practical test of how public projects balance nighttime visibility with efforts to limit light pollution. new-hampshire new-hampshire new hampshire nh concord concord, nh concord light pollution state house parking

nh-concord-library-132-year-overdue-book.excerpt: A Barrington man returned an 1894 magazine after spotting the library’s year-long fine freeze; archivists hope to display it in the Concord Room.
nh-concord-library-132-year-overdue-book.text: concord library receives book overdue by more than 132 years a barrington man returned an 1894 magazine after spotting the library’s year-long fine freeze; archivists hope to display it in the concord room. a piece of concord public library history has come home after 48,220 days: a bound magazine checked out in 1894 and returned this month by a barrington resident who had kept it on a bookshelf for decades. john hanson told the concord monitor he did not know how the volume entered his family’s possession. the item is the september 1894 issue of “the century illustrated monthly magazine,” still bearing the library’s markings and a one-week lending notice. hanson decided to return it after reading that the library had started a year-long freeze on overdue fines. by the monitor’s calculation, the periodical would have accumulated $12,055 in penalties under a daily fine, although the library would not have charged him. staff verified the date, issue number and bookplate to confirm that the copy had not simply been removed from circulation. the library does not plan to lend the fragile magazine again. instead, archivists hope to display it in the concord room, which houses local historical material. the episode gives the fine-free initiative an unusually tangible result and leaves staff with a mystery: who borrowed the magazine more than a century ago, and how it traveled from concord to hanson’s shelves. new-hampshire new-hampshire new hampshire nh concord concord, new hampshire concord libraries history new hampshire

nh-concord-library-132-year-overdue-maga.excerpt: A September 1894 periodical came home after 48,220 days, with its notional $12,055 fine erased by a fine freeze.
nh-concord-library-132-year-overdue-maga.text: 132-year-overdue magazine returns to concord public library a september 1894 periodical came home after 48,220 days, with its notional $12,055 fine erased by a fine freeze. a magazine checked out from the concord public library in september 1894 has returned after 48,220 days, or more than 132 years. john hanson, a barrington resident who previously lived in boscawen, brought back the september 1894 issue of “the century illustrated monthly magazine.” library staff verified the date, issue and institutional bookplate. at the old rate of 25 cents a day, the overdue charge would have reached $12,055. hanson avoided that theoretical bill because the library had frozen overdue fines for a year, a policy intended to reduce barriers to returning materials and using library services. the periodical will not go back into ordinary circulation. instead, the library plans to display it in the concord room, where local-history materials are kept. the return turns an unusually long loan into a tangible link with the city’s nineteenth-century readers while also giving the library’s fine-free period a memorable result. the unusual return also drew statewide attention. new-hampshire new-hampshire new hampshire new hampshire concord concord, new hampshire concord public library libraries history concord

nh-concord-memorial-field-plan-2026.excerpt: A joint city-school committee backed a two-phase renovation proposal, sending the project toward public hearings and votes by local governing bodies.
nh-concord-memorial-field-plan-2026.text: concord panel advances $22.4 million memorial field plan a joint city-school committee backed a two-phase renovation proposal, sending the project toward public hearings and votes by local governing bodies. a joint concord city-school committee has voted to advance a $22.4 million plan for renovating memorial field, moving the long-discussed project closer to public review and final decisions by the city council and school board. the concord monitor reported that the committee approved the proposal, called “new option a,” by a 3-1 vote. the plan is about $8.5 million less than an earlier concept and divides the work into two stages. a first phase estimated at $13.9 million, including contingencies, would rebuild and expand the track, install an artificial-turf field, add roughly 1,000 to 1,500 bleacher seats and address drainage. a second phase, estimated at $8.5 million, would complete additional improvements. the next steps are expected to include a public hearing, likely in october or november, followed by separate consideration from city and school officials. if financing and approvals line up, the first phase could take about two years. the phased approach gives concord a way to address the field’s core athletic and infrastructure needs while leaving later work dependent on funding and future votes. new-hampshire nh concord, new hampshire concord memorial field schools infrastructure

nh-concord-science-cafe-ai-return-2026.excerpt: The free September 15 session will bring UNH and Dartmouth humanities scholars to Litherman’s Limited for questions about artificial intelligence.
nh-concord-science-cafe-ai-return-2026.text: concord science cafe returns with public conversation about ai the free september 15 session will bring unh and dartmouth humanities scholars to litherman’s limited for questions about artificial intelligence. science cafe is returning to concord for a one-night public discussion focused on artificial intelligence. the free event is scheduled for tuesday, september 15, from 6 to 8 p.m. at litherman’s limited brewery, 126 hall street, the concord monitor reported. the format places expert panelists at a table to answer questions from attendees instead of presenting a formal lecture. organizers expect the conversation to examine how ai works, where it falls short and how it could affect work, education and daily life. food and beverages will be available, and organizers advised arriving early because of strong interest. the panelists are nicholas smith, a university of new hampshire philosophy professor, and james dobson, a dartmouth college english professor and writing-program director. smith has worked with a unh summer program on governing ai, while dobson has served as a special adviser to dartmouth’s provost on the technology. science cafe held recurring sessions in concord before the pandemic. this gathering is not a restart of the old monthly schedule, though organizers said future one-off events remain possible. similar public science conversations continue in nashua and manchester. new-hampshire new-hampshire new hampshire new hampshire concord concord, new hampshire concord artificial intelligence science cafe unh dartmouth

nh-crypto-atm-protections-december-2026-.excerpt: New Hampshire’s new cryptocurrency ATM rules will add transaction limits, a first-use delay and a fraud-refund process beginning Dec. 16.
nh-crypto-atm-protections-december-2026-.text: new hampshire crypto atm protections set to take effect in december new hampshire’s new cryptocurrency atm rules will add transaction limits, a first-use delay and a fraud-refund process beginning dec. 16. new hampshire’s new protections for cryptocurrency atm customers are scheduled to take effect dec. 16, giving residents additional safeguards as officials try to curb scams that direct people to send money through kiosks. the law limits a customer’s cryptocurrency atm transactions to $2,000 per day. for a customer’s first transaction, the operator must hold the transaction for at least 48 hours, during which the customer can cancel it and receive a refund. operators also must display fraud warnings, disclose fees and exchange-rate spreads, provide receipts and use prompts or other measures designed to identify suspicious transactions. a customer seeking a fraud refund generally must contact the operator and law enforcement within 14 days. the rules do not make every cryptocurrency payment reversible, but they create a defined process for transactions made through covered kiosks. the changes follow warnings about impersonation and other scams in which victims are told to convert cash into cryptocurrency and transfer it immediately. new-hampshire new-hampshire new hampshire new hampshire new hampshire new hampshire cryptocurrency consumer protection

nh-dartmouth-health-golisano-childrens-g.excerpt: Tom Golisano’s donation, the largest in Dartmouth Health history, will support pediatric staffing, renovations and expanded southern New Hampshire care.
nh-dartmouth-health-golisano-childrens-g.text: $30 million gift will rename and expand new hampshire’s children’s hospital tom golisano’s donation, the largest in dartmouth health history, will support pediatric staffing, renovations and expanded southern new hampshire care. dartmouth health children’s has received a $30 million gift from entrepreneur and philanthropist tom golisano, the largest philanthropic contribution in dartmouth health’s history. the children’s hospital at dartmouth will be renamed golisano children’s hospital at dartmouth health in perpetuity, linking the lebanon-based hospital to a national alliance of pediatric institutions supported by golisano. dartmouth health said the funding will strengthen the pediatric workforce, modernize facilities and expand access to care in southern new hampshire. planned work includes renovations to the intensive care nursery and pediatric critical-care areas. the gift also is expected to help the system recruit and retain specialists while bringing more services closer to families who now travel farther north for appointments. the hospital serves as new hampshire’s only full-service children’s hospital and provides specialty care across the region. joining the golisano children’s alliance gives its clinicians another channel for sharing practices and collaborating with other pediatric centers. dartmouth health said the investment is intended to improve both the physical care environment and the long-term capacity of programs serving children and families throughout northern new england. new-hampshire new-hampshire new hampshire new hampshire lebanon lebanon, new hampshire dartmouth health children's hospital at dartmouth tom golisano pediatric care lebanon

nh-dartmouth-health-staff-reductions-202.excerpt: The New Hampshire health system says rising operating costs and slower, lower insurance payments drove a restructuring that also affects several programs.
nh-dartmouth-health-staff-reductions-202.text: dartmouth health eliminates 124 positions and cancels 303 openings the new hampshire health system says rising operating costs and slower, lower insurance payments drove a restructuring that also affects several programs. dartmouth health eliminated 124 filled positions and canceled 303 open positions this week as the new hampshire-based health system restructures operations, according to a sept. 15 announcement. the changes affect dartmouth hitchcock medical center and dartmouth hitchcock clinics southern region. dartmouth health said operating expenses have grown 12% as labor, supply and drug costs rise while insurers pay less and take longer to pay. the system said it is also ending or restructuring tele-icu and tele-ed services, winding down the new england alliance for health as its members have joined larger systems, and outsourcing its lean six sigma employee training programs. leaders said they are working with affected facilities on alternative care plans for patients who use the telehealth services. dartmouth health said the affected employees will receive transition resources and can pursue other roles within the system. the organization says it has more than 16,000 employees and includes eight member hospitals plus clinics across new hampshire and vermont. new-hampshire new-hampshire new hampshire nh lebanon dartmouth health, lebanon, new hampshire new hampshire dartmouth health health care jobs

nh-dartmouth-udebhulu-holy-cross-soccer-.excerpt: Freshman Tasha Udebhulu broke a scoreless tie late at Burnham Field, giving the Big Green a 1-0 victory and a second straight win.
nh-dartmouth-udebhulu-holy-cross-soccer-.text: udebhulu’s first college goal lifts dartmouth over holy cross freshman tasha udebhulu broke a scoreless tie late at burnham field, giving the big green a 1-0 victory and a second straight win. freshman tasha udebhulu scored her first collegiate goal with a little more than 15 minutes remaining, lifting dartmouth women’s soccer to a 1-0 win over holy cross at burnham field. the result gave the big green a second consecutive victory and stopped a crusaders team that arrived in hanover on a four-game winning streak. the decisive chance began when an attempted clearance by the holy cross goalkeeper deflected off udebhulu just outside the penalty area. the guildford, england, native collected the loose ball, moved around the goalkeeper and eluded recovering defenders before finishing for the only goal of the match. dartmouth improved to 4-1-2 after creating more pressure following halftime. holy cross held a 6-3 advantage in shots during the opening half, but the big green produced eight attempts in the second. the late breakthrough rewarded that shift while the dartmouth defense preserved the shutout. the team’s next scheduled match is a sunday home date with colgate. new-hampshire new-hampshire new hampshire nh hanover hanover, new hampshire dartmouth college women’s soccer tasha udebhulu holy cross hanover

nh-dartmouth-volleyball-northeastern-car.excerpt: Jaida Cekic and Audrey Kalorin reached personal bests as the Big Green fell in four sets at the Ellis Rowland Memorial Tournament.
nh-dartmouth-volleyball-northeastern-car.text: dartmouth freshmen post career highs in loss to northeastern jaida cekic and audrey kalorin reached personal bests as the big green fell in four sets at the ellis rowland memorial tournament. dartmouth volleyball fell to northeastern in four sets saturday at the ellis rowland memorial tournament in hamilton, new york, but two first-year players delivered career-best performances. the huskies won 25-21, 25-16, 12-25 and 25-15, dropping the big green to 3-2. jaida cekic finished with career highs of six kills, three service aces, three total blocks and 11 points. audrey kalorin matched her career best with 12 assists and added three kills. elle mccreery led dartmouth with 12.5 points, recording nine kills on .571 hitting and four blocks, while riley imamura supplied seven kills and a team-high 10 digs. dartmouth out-hit northeastern .226 to .182 and held an 8-5 edge in blocks. its best stretch came in the third set, when the big green took control early and won by 13 points to extend the match. northeastern answered in the fourth. dartmouth remains at the tournament for a sunday match against host colgate. new-hampshire new-hampshire new hampshire new hampshire hanover hanover, new hampshire dartmouth volleyball northeastern college sports

nh-dartmouth-womens-rugby-life-2026.excerpt: The Big Green reached halftime level with the Running Eagles before Life created separation in the second half in Hanover.
nh-dartmouth-womens-rugby-life-2026.text: life university pulls away from dartmouth women’s rugby, 49-22 the big green reached halftime level with the running eagles before life created separation in the second half in hanover. dartmouth women’s rugby went into halftime tied with life university on saturday before the running eagles pulled away for a 49-22 victory in hanover. the final score ended a competitive opening half in which the big green stayed level with a nationally prominent opponent before life created a decisive margin after the break. the result was posted by dartmouth athletics along with postgame interviews from head coach katie dowty and vasiti turagavou. life’s 27-point winning margin reflects how sharply the match changed in the second half, after dartmouth had matched the visitors through the first 40 minutes. the contest was one of the big green’s first home tests of the fall schedule. for dartmouth, the takeaway is the contrast between a balanced first half and the pressure life applied after halftime. the big green now have a clear benchmark as the season moves forward: sustain the structure and physical response that kept saturday’s match even, while limiting the stretches that allowed the running eagles to build distance on the scoreboard. new-hampshire new-hampshire new hampshire new hampshire hanover hanover, new hampshire dartmouth women’s rugby life university hanover

nh-democrats-unity-after-primary-2026.excerpt: Party leaders and nominees opened the general-election campaign with a unity event one day after New Hampshire’s state primary.
nh-democrats-unity-after-primary-2026.text: new hampshire democrats turn to unity after state primary party leaders and nominees opened the general-election campaign with a unity event one day after new hampshire’s state primary. new hampshire democrats moved quickly from intraparty competition to the general election wednesday morning, gathering at saint anselm college for a kickoff breakfast one day after the state primary. party leaders and nominees used the event at the new hampshire institute of politics to urge supporters of losing candidates to unite behind the full democratic ticket. the message followed months of contested races, including a close 1st congressional district primary won by stefany shaheen and the u.s. senate primary won by chris pappas. state party chair ray buckley said democratic primary participation exceeded expectations and that more democratic than republican ballots were cast in a new hampshire state primary for the first time since 2018. manchester ink link reported that the program also emphasized protecting social security and other programs democrats say republicans may target. gubernatorial nominee cinde warmington drew on her own experience from a difficult 2024 primary while encouraging the party to bring rival campaigns back together. shaheen and pappas also recognized their former opponents. the nominees now have less than eight weeks to organize for the november 3 general election. new-hampshire new-hampshire new hampshire nh goffstown goffstown, nh new hampshire politics 2026 election general election saint anselm college

nh-dilorenzo-wins-gop-house-primary-2026.text: anthony dilorenzo wins gop primary for open new hampshire house seat the trump-backed businessman advances in the race to replace rep. chris pappas in the 1st congressional district. anthony dilorenzo won the republican primary tuesday for new hampshire’s open 1st congressional district seat, advancing to the november election in one of the state’s most competitive federal races. the associated press called the race for dilorenzo, a businessman making his first run for office. he received president donald trump’s endorsement during a crowded republican contest that also included brian cole, hollie noveletsky and other candidates. the seat is open because democratic rep. chris pappas ran for u.s. senate rather than seeking another house term. the district includes manchester, much of the seacoast and communities extending into the lakes region, making it geographically and politically varied. the democratic primary had not been called in the ap report used for this update. election-night totals remain unofficial until new hampshire completes its canvass, but the republican result gives dilorenzo a short general-election runway before nov. 3. the race will determine who succeeds pappas in the closely watched district. new-hampshire nh new hampshire 1st congressional district new hampshire nh-01 elections u.s. house

nh-doj-demands-2024-ballot-retention-202.text: federal justice department tells new hampshire to retain 2024 ballots the state says the request cites unspecified litigation and provides no factual or legal basis for suggesting new hampshire violated election law. the u.s. justice department has directed new hampshire to preserve paper ballots and electronic records from the 2024 election beyond the state’s normal retention period, according to a letter reported by new hampshire public radio. the september 4 letter instructed secretary of state david scanlan to retain all hard-copy ballots, citing ongoing litigation without identifying a case. new hampshire municipalities ordinarily may destroy paper ballots 22 months after an election. similar federal instructions have reportedly gone to at least 30 states. scanlan subsequently told local election officials to preserve all 2024 ballots and related records. he said the federal government had supplied no factual or legal basis for the demand and emphasized that the ballots remain confidential. any future request to inspect or copy them would be evaluated individually, he said. the federal letter also sought preservation of electronic election records and referred to potential civil rights act violations without presenting evidence. state officials said they had no basis to believe new hampshire violated election law. the request arrives just after the state primary, which officials said proceeded without significant problems. new-hampshire new-hampshire new hampshire new hampshire concord concord, nh 2024 election ballots new hampshire justice department

nh-dover-911-memorial-dedication-2026.text: dover to dedicate permanent 9/11 memorial on 25th anniversary the city plans an 11 a.m. remembrance ceremony friday in the cocheco mill courtyard, where its new memorial will be dedicated. dover will dedicate a new permanent 9/11 memorial friday as the city marks 25 years since the september 11, 2001, terrorist attacks. the remembrance ceremony is scheduled for 11 a.m. september 11 in the cocheco mill courtyard on central avenue, according to a city announcement posted tuesday. the dedication gives dover a fixed public site for future remembrance in addition to this year’s anniversary program. the timing places the local ceremony within a week of memorial events across new hampshire and the country. dover’s announcement centers its observance on both remembrance and the formal unveiling of the memorial rather than a temporary display. residents planning to attend should check the city’s event notice for any logistical updates before traveling downtown. the city had not described a weather alternative or changes to the 11 a.m. start in the posted notice. the event comes on a milestone anniversary when communities are also considering how to preserve firsthand memory for younger residents who were born after the attacks. new-hampshire new-hampshire new hampshire nh dover dover, new hampshire dover september 11 memorial community

nh-dover-september-11-memorial-unveiling.text: dover prepares to unveil september 11 memorial honoring four local lives the 11-foot granite memorial in the cocheco mill courtyard is designed as both a place of remembrance and an educational destination. dover will formally unveil a new september 11 memorial friday, marking the 25th anniversary of the attacks with a permanent downtown tribute. the 11-foot structure, built from granite panels, stands in the cocheco mill courtyard and honors all those who died, including four people with ties to dover. the project grew from discussions among city leaders, current and former mayors, police and fire chiefs, and former fire chief perry plummer. plummer told new hampshire public radio that the group initially considered a smaller memorial in a cemetery. community interest expanded the plan, and organizers raised nearly $200,000 in private community support over the past year. an information board beside the monument includes photographs of the four people connected to dover, explains those connections and presents a timeline of the attacks. organizers say the display is intended to support school visits as well as private reflection, giving younger residents who did not experience 2001 a place to learn about the day and its lasting effects. the courtyard also carries local significance because dover held its first remembrance ceremony there shortly after the attacks. annual observances have continued through dover fire and rescue, and the new memorial gives those ceremonies a permanent focal point in the center of the city. new-hampshire new-hampshire new hampshire nh dover dover, nh dover september 11 memorial cocheco mill courtyard

nh-epsom-water-district-pfas-staffing-20.text: epsom water district staffing crisis stalls pfas remediation a one-member board and vacant administrative posts are delaying bids for a treatment project while the district weighs whether the town should assume control. the epsom village water district is operating with one commissioner and no clerk, secretary or treasurer, a staffing crisis that is delaying a planned pfas treatment project and raising questions about the district’s future. commissioner donna dudley is the only remaining member of the board after a second commissioner resigned in august. the district serves about 320 connections and roughly 800 people, including epsom central school, the town hall, library, fire department and other public buildings. its system also supplies water to local fire hydrants. the vacancies make it difficult to assemble a quorum, approve engineering work and move the pfas project to bidding. residents are also confronting higher operating costs: the town’s annual hydrant rental charge rose from $9,000 to $40,000, according to the concord monitor. a public meeting is scheduled for september 21 at 6 p.m. at epsom central school with town selectmen, state environmental officials and residents. one option under discussion is dissolving the village district and transferring the system to the town, a change that would require voter approval. until governance is stabilized, the treatment project and other decisions remain constrained. new-hampshire new-hampshire new hampshire nh epsom epsom, nh epsom pfas drinking water local government

nh-faith-based-childcare-growth-closures.excerpt: Church-based providers are expanding care in some communities while closures and shared-building changes expose operational risks.
nh-faith-based-childcare-growth-closures.text: faith-based childcare programs navigate growth and closures in new hampshire church-based providers are expanding care in some communities while closures and shared-building changes expose operational risks. faith-based childcare programs are helping cover gaps in new hampshire’s limited care network, but recent changes show how closely their futures can be tied to the churches that house them. emmanuel child care center in rochester closed aug. 28 after 37 years when emmanuel church decided to use the space for an expanding food pantry. other church-based providers are growing. kids by the common, located at londonderry presbyterian church, expanded from two classrooms to six in 2024 and increased enrollment from 27 children to 62 in about a year and a half. the program offers infant, toddler and preschool care and had long provided full-day kindergarten before londonderry public schools began offering it this year. little blessings in northwood rents space from st. joseph’s catholic church and teaches a nondenominational christian curriculum. its operator said enrollment fell after the church opened a prekindergarten-through-eighth-grade school in the same building. both little blessings and kids by the common are state licensed, accept state childcare assistance and follow state early-learning standards. their different trajectories illustrate both the access these programs provide and the operational uncertainty that can accompany shared religious facilities and thin childcare margins. new-hampshire new-hampshire new hampshire new hampshire rochester new hampshire childcare rochester londonderry early education

nh-fisher-cats-harrisburg-8-0-loss-2026.text: fisher cats strike out 13 but fall 8-0 to harrisburg new hampshire’s pitchers piled up strikeouts thursday, while the offense was shut out in an 8-0 defeat during the final homestand. the new hampshire fisher cats were shut out 8-0 by the harrisburg senators on thursday, even as the home pitching staff recorded 13 strikeouts. the result came during new hampshire’s final homestand of the season at delta dental stadium in manchester. the strikeout total was the clearest positive in a game controlled by harrisburg. new hampshire’s pitchers repeatedly generated swing-and-miss outs, but the senators still built enough offense to separate. without run support, every harrisburg scoring inning carried added weight as the game moved along. for the fisher cats, the final score underscored the difference between isolated pitching success and a complete team result. strikeouts can limit balls in play and prevent runners from advancing, but they cannot offset walks, hits or defensive pressure when the lineup is unable to answer on the scoreboard. the club’s closing homestand continues through the weekend, giving new hampshire another opportunity to respond before the home schedule ends. the series also offers local fans a final look at the double-a roster in manchester, where individual development remains important even when the team result is one-sided. new-hampshire new-hampshire new hampshire new hampshire manchester manchester, new hampshire new hampshire fisher cats harrisburg senators baseball manchester

nh-flags-half-staff-september-11-anniver.text: new hampshire lowers public flags for september 11 anniversary flags on state public buildings and grounds were directed to remain at half-staff from sunrise through sunset friday. flags on new hampshire public buildings and grounds were lowered to half-staff friday as the state observed 25 years since the september 11, 2001 terrorist attacks. gov. kelly ayotte issued the directive thursday, setting the observance from sunrise until sunset on september 11. the order applied across state-owned public facilities and accompanied remembrance events organized by cities, towns, fire departments and veterans groups. new hampshire lost 42 people in the attacks, according to anniversary reporting by state broadcasters. communities held ceremonies throughout the day, including memorial dedications in dover and meredith and traditional moments of silence tied to the times the hijacked aircraft struck the world trade center and pentagon and crashed in pennsylvania. the flag order did not add new closures or service changes. its purpose was ceremonial: creating a visible statewide marker while local communities remembered residents, first responders and military members connected to the attacks and their aftermath. flags were scheduled to return to full staff after sunset friday. new-hampshire new-hampshire new hampshire new hampshire concord concord, new hampshire new hampshire september 11 flags half-staff remembrance

nh-grocery-snapshot-september-tariff-wat.text: new hampshire grocery snapshot tracks small september rise before tariff effects a manchester price-tracking column found only five changes in its monthly basket, while warning that new canadian tariffs could raise packaging and input costs. a monthly manchester grocery-price snapshot found a relatively quiet september shopping trip, with three tracked products declining and two increasing. the basket’s total cost was 0.23% above august and 3.25% higher than the column’s first trip in april 2025. manchester ink link emphasized that the exercise follows one shopper’s recurring list at one store and is not a scientific measure of statewide food inflation. in the september sample, avocados, mandarin oranges and fat-free milk declined, while a favorite ice cream and a bag of dry cat food increased. the larger concern is what may happen after a new 50% tariff on canadian imports. the report identified wood pulp used in paper goods, packaging, dairy inputs and equipment for maple producers as areas where higher import costs could eventually reach new hampshire shoppers and businesses. because those effects were not yet visible in the september trip, the current figures should be read as a dated local snapshot rather than a forecast. the next monthly comparison will offer an early check on whether tariff-related costs are beginning to appear on store shelves. new-hampshire new-hampshire new hampshire nh manchester manchester, nh groceries tariffs manchester cost of living

nh-gulf-maine-microbial-kelp-shift-2026.text: gulf of maine study tracks microbial shifts as kelp forests retreat researchers found that warming waters and the spread of invasive turf algae are changing microscopic communities on the seafloor, with uncertain effects on ecosystem recovery. microscopic life on the gulf of maine seafloor is changing as native kelp forests retreat and invasive red turf algae spread, according to research highlighted by new hampshire public radio and maine public. scientists from the university of maine and bigelow laboratory for ocean sciences examined microbial communities associated with the region’s changing underwater habitat. their study, published in the proceedings of the national academy of sciences, connects the shift to a gulf that is warming rapidly and becoming less favorable for some native kelp. kelp is a foundational species: its underwater forests provide structure, food and shelter for a wide range of marine life. when low-growing turf algae replace it, the visible habitat changes and so do the bacteria and other microbes living around it. those organisms help cycle nutrients and can influence whether an ecosystem resists disruption or recovers afterward. researchers said the long-term consequences are not yet clear, making continued monitoring important. the findings matter along new hampshire’s short coastline because the gulf functions as one connected system. changes first detected on the ocean floor can ultimately affect fisheries, water quality and coastal communities that depend on a healthy marine food web. new-hampshire new-hampshire new hampshire nh gulf of maine gulf of maine gulf of maine kelp climate marine science

nh-hopkinton-fair-young-cattle-handlers-.text: young handlers turn years of cattle training into hopkinton fair ribbons molly potter and rose defreitas brought four steers to the 2026 fair after building their skills through farm camp and year-round training. two young new hampshire cattle handlers turned years of practice into ribbons at the 2026 hopkinton state fair. molly potter and rose defreitas showed four steers after learning to work with cattle together at a summer camp run by miles smith farm in 2022. their preparation extended well beyond fair week. the pair worked with the animals through winter and spring, teaching them to walk calmly, respond to direction and remain composed around crowds. the calves came from huckins farm in bristol, and the project required the students to build trust with animals much larger than they are. potter comes from a family with deep agricultural roots and is described as a 13th-generation farmer. defreitas developed her interest through the farm program and the partnership the two formed there. their showing results reflected both technical handling and months of daily care. the experience also demonstrated how fairs connect young people with working agriculture: the ribbons are the visible result, but patience, safety and consistency are the skills developed long before an animal enters the ring. new-hampshire new-hampshire new hampshire new hampshire hopkinton hopkinton, new hampshire hopkinton fair agriculture youth cattle

nh-humanities-connections-recovery-grant.text: new hampshire literature program receives $25,000 recovery-services grant the connections program will use the funding to keep books and guided discussions available through treatment, correctional and community partners. new hampshire humanities has received $25,000 to support its connections reading program, which works with people in substance-use treatment, correctional settings and other community programs. nhpr reported that the award combines support from granite united way’s opioid abatement community grants program and the new hampshire charitable foundation’s alice hale penniman memorial fund. connections organizes guided book discussions and gives participants as many as four books that they can keep or share with children and other relatives. more than 600 people have participated, according to the program. its partnerships also extend to adult-education centers and organizations serving new americans and people with disabilities. program leaders said the grant will help protect direct services after the loss of federal funding reduced the operating budget by 25% last year. the money is intended for programming so host organizations and participants do not absorb that gap. the model uses literature as a practical tool for connection during treatment and major life transitions. organizers are also seeking discussion leaders who understand the communities being served, allowing the reading selections and conversations to reflect a wider range of experiences across new hampshire. new-hampshire new-hampshire new hampshire new hampshire new hampshire new hampshire humanities recovery services opioid response literacy

nh-imagination-library-statewide-bill-20.text: new hampshire senators plan statewide imagination library bill a bipartisan proposal would make free monthly books available to families with children from birth through age five across new hampshire. three new hampshire senators plan to file legislation this month to expand dolly parton’s imagination library statewide. the bipartisan group includes republican daryl abbas and democrats donovan fenton and suzanne prentiss, according to the concord monitor. the program mails an age-appropriate book each month to participating children from birth through age five. under the proposal, families throughout new hampshire could enroll without paying. the monitor reported an estimated state cost of about $750,000 per year. the imagination library would cover the books, while the state and nonprofit partners would share shipping and handling expenses. a hillsborough county effort called diane’s library offers a local model: it has distributed 66,000 books and enrolled more than 6,000 children since 2024. supporters are still moving from a regional program toward a legislative proposal, so details may change after the bill is filed and receives hearings. the lawmakers’ announcement begins that process; funding and statewide administration would still need approval through the legislature before the expansion could take effect. new-hampshire new-hampshire new hampshire nh concord new hampshire early childhood literacy imagination library new hampshire legislature

nh-keene-black-cloud-brewing-taproom-202.text: black cloud brewing gives keene taproom a new identity former modestman employees helped create the downtown taproom, where locally accented pizza shares the billing with a varied beer list. black cloud brewing co. is giving a familiar downtown keene taproom a new identity, combining beer made on site with a food menu built around thin-crust pizza. the brewery opened earlier this year at 100 main street in the former modestman brewing space after that business closed last summer. nbc10 boston reports that former modestman employees helped shape the new operation, which includes counter service, group seating, a quieter rear patio and views of brewing equipment. the beer list spans a hazy new england ipa, a german-style black lager, a fruited sour, a pale ale and an american red ale, offering a wider range than a single-style taproom. the kitchen uses a high-temperature ventless conveyor oven to produce neapolitan-style pizza with a charred thin crust. locally sourced toppings, vegan options and a hot-maple drizzle made with syrup from saxtons river, vermont, give the menu a regional accent. pickled vegetables, olives, pretzel bites, popcorn and salads round out the food choices. the opening keeps brewing activity in a prominent main street location while adding another gathering place for residents, visitors and the city’s college community. new-hampshire new-hampshire new hampshire new hampshire keene keene, new hampshire keene breweries restaurants small business monadnock region

nh-kimball-castle-fire-teen-charges-2026.text: two teenagers charged in fire that damaged historic kimball castle state fire investigators announced felony charges against two teenagers more than a year after flames badly damaged the historic lake winnipesaukee landmark. two teenagers have been charged in connection with the fire that badly damaged kimball castle in gilford last year, the new hampshire state fire marshal announced friday. joshua pittman, 18, of dover, faces a felony conspiracy-to-commit-arson charge and misdemeanor criminal trespass. peyton eastman, 19, of portsmouth, faces felony arson and misdemeanor criminal trespass. the august 27, 2025, fire was treated as suspicious after flames swept through the historic stone property. investigators said the building was damaged so severely that demolition was expected. the castle, built in the late 1890s and listed on the national register of historic places since 1982, is a familiar landmark overlooking lake winnipesaukee. authorities arrested pittman on september 1 and eastman on september 2 before announcing the charges friday. both were released on personal recognizance and are scheduled for arraignment october 8 in laconia district court. the filings are accusations, and the defendants are presumed innocent unless proven guilty. officials did not announce a motive or disclose additional details about how investigators connected the two teenagers to the fire. new-hampshire new-hampshire new hampshire nh gilford gilford, nh gilford kimball castle arson new hampshire public safety

nh-laconia-motorcycle-crash-three-killed.text: three people killed, including massachusetts man, in laconia motorcycle crash authorities say three people died and a fourth person suffered life-threatening injuries in a late-night crash involving motorcycles near route 3 in laconia. three people were killed and a fourth person was seriously injured in a late-night motorcycle crash in laconia, according to reporting by boston 25 news. the collision happened around 11 p.m. near route 3 and the looney bin. the people who died were identified as cameron mosher, 28, of dennis, massachusetts; miles collette, 32, of gilford; and jeanine fereshetian, 33, of laconia. a fourth woman was taken to concord hospital with life-threatening injuries. authorities said there were no immediate indications that speed or alcohol played a role. the crash remained under investigation monday, and the report did not identify any additional charges or explain what led the motorcycles to collide. the incident is a significant loss for both the lakes region and the massachusetts community where mosher lived. the report did not indicate whether weather or road conditions contributed, and officials had not released a fuller reconstruction of the crash. new-hampshire new-hampshire new hampshire new hampshire laconia laconia, new hampshire laconia motorcycle crash lake winnipesaukee new hampshire

nh-libby-museum-preservation-vote-2026.text: wolfeboro selectmen reject demolition of libby museum the board voted to keep the historic natural-history museum standing and begin work toward new stewardship after strong public support for preservation. wolfeboro selectmen have rejected demolition of the libby museum and agreed to pursue a path that could place the historic building under new stewardship. the vote followed two public hearings in august where residents strongly supported preserving the structure. board members also agreed to seek a meeting with the new hampshire attorney general’s charitable trusts unit and local preservation groups to map out the required legal process. a newly formed libby museum preservation society wants to become the successor trustee through carroll county probate court and use private funding to restore or rebuild the property while continuing its natural-history mission. the museum opened in 1912 and its building has been closed since 2024 because of mold, structural deterioration and deferred maintenance. the decision keeps the building standing, but it does not by itself reopen the museum or settle who will manage it. officials still must address the collection, restoration costs and court approvals. the board’s immediate action removes demolition as the preferred option and creates room for a preservation plan. new-hampshire nh wolfeboro, new hampshire wolfeboro libby museum historic preservation lake winnipesaukee

nh-license-plate-reader-privacy-law-2026.excerpt: As other states revisit automated plate surveillance, New Hampshire's law limits eligible uses and requires most scans to be destroyed within three minutes.
nh-license-plate-reader-privacy-law-2026.text: new hampshire's tight license-plate reader rules draw fresh national attention as other states revisit automated plate surveillance, new hampshire's law limits eligible uses and requires most scans to be destroyed within three minutes. new hampshire's decade-old limits on automated license-plate readers are drawing renewed attention as states around the country debate how much vehicle-tracking technology police should be allowed to use. the new hampshire bulletin reported thursday that florida gov. ron desantis recently pointed to the granite state as a model for tighter rules. under rsa 261:75-b, new hampshire allows automated plate readers for local, county and state law-enforcement agencies, but only for specified purposes such as identifying stolen vehicles, vehicles linked to warrants or serious crimes, and vehicles connected to missing or endangered people. most plate records must be purged within three minutes unless a scan leads to an arrest, citation, protective-custody action or a missing-person or wanted-person match. the law also says a reader cannot be capable of recording images of a vehicle's occupants, and a positive match by itself is not enough to justify a traffic stop. agencies must register the devices with the department of safety, train users and follow the statute's limits. privacy researchers quoted by the bulletin described the framework as among the nation's most restrictive. the rules do not eliminate every form of plate-data access. the bulletin reported that new hampshire agencies can still use contracts to query databases operated elsewhere, while lawmakers are considering whether additional legislation is needed. the renewed debate comes as states including florida, arizona, connecticut and south dakota examine limits on systems marketed by companies such as flock, axon and motorola solutions. new-hampshire new-hampshire new hampshire nh concord new hampshire new nh-loudon-pentagon-survivor-september-11.text: loudon pentagon survivor marks 25 years since september 11 retired public-affairs officer john donovan is preserving memories of colleagues lost at the pentagon and contributing to a forthcoming survivor history. a loudon resident who survived the september 11 attack on the pentagon is marking the tragedy’s 25th anniversary by preserving the memories of colleagues and urging younger generations not to let the day fade into abstraction. john donovan spent 22 years as a public-affairs officer at the pentagon. he told the concord monitor that he was in a meeting when american airlines flight 77 struck the building on september 11, 2001. donovan and coworkers escaped through a nearby corridor. he later learned that 35 people he knew through his work had died. donovan, who grew up in concord, served in the army during the vietnam war and worked in journalism before reaching the pentagon. he remained there until 2007, then returned to new hampshire and continued participating in annual remembrance ceremonies. his account will also appear in a forthcoming collection of survivor memories being assembled by two other military officers who lived through the attack. donovan’s chapter focuses on the people he lost and on the public-affairs team’s return to work after the damaged section was rebuilt. the project adds a distinctly new hampshire voice to the record of a day that killed 125 people inside the pentagon. new-hampshire new-hampshire new hampshire nh loudon loudon, new hampshire loudon september 11 pentagon new hampshire

nh-mail-ballot-rules-supreme-court-2026.excerpt: David Scanlan and election officials from five other states say late federal changes could disrupt voting already underway.
nh-mail-ballot-rules-supreme-court-2026.text: new hampshire joins states seeking pause on new mail-ballot rules david scanlan and election officials from five other states say late federal changes could disrupt voting already underway. new hampshire secretary of state david scanlan has joined election officials from five other republican-led states in asking the u.s. supreme court to keep new federal mail-ballot rules from taking effect during the 2026 election. their filing focuses on the disruption that late procedural changes could create, not on the underlying policy dispute. the officials represent new hampshire, kentucky, north dakota, south dakota, georgia and kansas. they argue that election administrators are already carrying out the midterm calendar and that new requirements could confuse voters and local officials. some absentee ballots have already been issued, while federal law requires ballots for military and overseas voters to be sent by september 19. the dispute follows a march executive order and related u.s. postal service rules. the proposed changes include sharing voter information with the postal service and procedures that officials say could cause mailed ballots to be rejected over processing errors. a federal court in massachusetts blocked part of the rules, prompting the administration to seek supreme court intervention. the state officials told the court they were taking no position on the rules’ legality or goals while urging stability this close to voting. new-hampshire new-hampshire new hampshire new hampshire concord concord, new hampshire mail voting david scanlan u.s. supreme court 2026 election

nh-manchester-aggravated-dui-crash-toddl.excerpt: Court documents say a Monday collision left a 1-year-old with a fractured skull and her mother and several others injured.
nh-manchester-aggravated-dui-crash-toddl.text: manchester woman charged with aggravated dui after crash injures toddler court documents say a monday collision left a 1-year-old with a fractured skull and her mother and several others injured. manchester police have charged a 24-year-old woman with aggravated driving under the influence and endangering the welfare of a child after a monday evening crash that seriously injured her 1-year-old daughter. according to court documents reported by manchester ink link, brianne gonzalez was driving a toyota rav4 south on belmont street when it went through a stop sign and collided with a cadillac traveling west on hanover street. the rav4 rolled onto its side, ejecting gonzalez while the toddler remained trapped inside. both mother and child suffered brain bleeds. the child also sustained a fractured skull and was airlifted from elliot hospital to boston children’s hospital. two other occupants of the rav4 and the cadillac driver were also taken to hospitals. gonzalez remained hospitalized when the charges were filed. an arrest affidavit said a blood draw taken shortly after the crash showed a blood-alcohol concentration of .246. bail was set on personal recognizance with restrictions on contact with the child unless supervised by a sober adult over 25. manchester’s collision analysis reconstruction team continues to investigate the crash. new-hampshire new-hampshire new hampshire nh manchester manchester, nh manchester aggravated dui traffic crash child safety

nh-manchester-first-month-no-suspected-o.excerpt: American Medical Response reported that Manchester completed its first month in 140 months without a suspected overdose fatality.
nh-manchester-first-month-no-suspected-o.text: manchester records first month without a suspected overdose death since 2015 american medical response reported that manchester completed its first month in 140 months without a suspected overdose fatality. manchester completed its first month without a suspected overdose fatality since 2015, according to a report from american medical response announced by the city. the city described the result as the first such month in 140 months. officials credited coordinated work by emergency medical crews, police, firefighters, public-health teams, treatment providers and recovery organizations, while emphasizing that the opioid crisis remains an active threat. the milestone concerns suspected overdose deaths reported for the month, not a declaration that the crisis is over or that all cases have completed final review. a single month also does not establish a lasting trend. even so, the absence of a suspected fatality marks a notable break from more than a decade of continuous loss. manchester said continued prevention, rapid response and recovery support remain necessary. the city directed people seeking substance-use treatment to new hampshire’s doorway program through 211 and reminded residents to call 911 for a suspected overdose. future monthly data will show whether the improvement is sustained. new-hampshire new-hampshire new hampshire nh manchester manchester, new hampshire manchester overdose prevention public health recovery

nh-manchester-hanover-belmont-crash-2026.text: manchester crash seriously injures driver and juvenile passenger police say a two-car collision at hanover and belmont streets sent multiple people to hospitals sunday evening. a two-car crash at hanover and belmont streets in manchester left a driver and a juvenile passenger with serious injuries sunday evening, according to a report from manchester ink link. the collision happened at about 6 p.m. and involved a 2003 toyota rav4 and a 2011 cadillac dts. police said the toyota was driven by a 24-year-old manchester woman. she and the juvenile were taken to hospitals with serious injuries. two other passengers in the toyota, women ages 21 and 20, suffered injuries described as minor. the cadillac’s driver, a 49-year-old manchester man, was also injured and taken to a hospital. authorities had not publicly released the identities of those involved. the crash remained under investigation, and officials had not announced a cause in the initial report. drivers should treat the intersection as a reminder to use added caution on heavily traveled city streets, particularly during evening hours when visibility and traffic patterns can change quickly. new-hampshire new-hampshire new hampshire nh manchester manchester, nh manchester traffic crash hanover street public safety

nh-manchester-mark-stebbins-community-ce.text: mark stebbins community center opens on manchester’s west side the $20.7 million center combines youth programs, health care, a food pantry and nonprofit support under one roof. the mark stebbins community center has opened on manchester’s west side, bringing youth programs, health care and family services together in one building. the boys & girls clubs of greater manchester and amoskeag health are anchor tenants, creating a shared location for services that had previously operated through separate organizations. the center will offer after-school programming, affordable health care, a food pantry, meeting space, community navigators and referrals to other nonprofit support. its fundraising campaign collected $20.7 million, exceeding an $18.5 million goal after the catholic health care foundation of greater manchester announced a $1 million pledge. the total includes an endowment intended to support long-term operations and maintenance. the manchester housing and redevelopment authority provided roughly three acres through a 75-year lease priced at $10 a year, according to remarks at the opening. federal community project funding secured through the department of housing and urban development also supported the project. named for the late businessman and philanthropist mark stebbins, the center reflects his goal of helping west side children and families through coordinated services. with construction complete, the measure of success now shifts from fundraising to how consistently residents can reach and use those programs. new-hampshire new-hampshire new hampshire new hampshire manchester manchester, new hampshire manchester community center amoskeag health boys & girls clubs

nh-manchester-merci-boxcar-commemoration.excerpt: The New Hampshire car from France’s postwar Merci Train will open for tours during a September 27 ceremony on Reed Street.
nh-manchester-merci-boxcar-commemoration.text: manchester’s merci boxcar prepares for annual commemoration the new hampshire car from france’s postwar merci train will open for tours during a september 27 ceremony on reed street. manchester’s preserved merci boxcar will be the focus of an annual public commemoration on sunday, september 27. the ceremony is scheduled for 1 to 2 p.m. at the display building at 136 reed street. the grande voiture du new hampshire and the franco-american centre organize the event. central high school french and choir students are expected to perform the french and american national anthems, while visitors can tour the car and view photographs, newspaper clippings, military medals and other artifacts. france sent 49 railcars to the united states in 1949 as a gesture of thanks for the friendship train, a privately organized american relief effort that carried donated food and supplies to europe after world war ii. the cars were known as “40 and 8” cars because they had been designed to carry 40 soldiers or eight horses. new hampshire’s car was initially displayed in concord before moving to manchester in 1953. organizers say only 35 of the original cars survive. the september ceremony gives residents a limited opportunity to see inside the protected car and connect a local landmark with the wider postwar exchange. new-hampshire new-hampshire new hampshire nh manchester manchester, nh manchester merci train world war ii franco-american history

nh-manchester-queen-city-bridge-closure-.text: manchester keeps queen city bridge closed as inspection continues the route 3 crossing over the merrimack river remains closed in both directions after possible structural deficiencies were found; overnight i-293 lane restrictions are planned as engineers continue work. manchester's queen city bridge remains closed in both directions while officials investigate possible structural deficiencies found during a routine inspection, the city said. the bridge carries route 3 over the merrimack river and connects the city's east and west sides near elliot hospital at river's edge. the new hampshire department of transportation notified manchester officials on sept. 21, and the city said a full inspection was not yet complete. new hampshire public radio reported that the bridge, built in 1923, spans 1,186 feet and was last rehabilitated in 2020. the closure is also affecting traffic near the crossing. the new hampshire department of transportation plans overnight i-293 lane restrictions in the bridge area on wednesday and thursday as inspectors continue their work, according to wmur. the work is scheduled for 9 p.m. to 5 a.m.; drivers entering southbound i-293 at exit 4 are to be detoured onto second street to exit 5. there is no announced reopening date. manchester is directing drivers to seek alternate routes while officials determine the extent of the problem and what repairs, if any, will be needed. new-hampshire new-hampshire new hampshire nh manchester manchester, new hampshire new hampshire manchester queen city bridge infrastructure traffic

nh-manchester-seal-biliteracy-record-202.text: manchester students help new hampshire seal of biliteracy reach record forty-eight manchester students earned the state distinction as new hampshire recognized its largest annual cohort since the program began. forty-eight manchester students earned new hampshire’s seal of biliteracy in 2026, contributing to the program’s largest statewide cohort since it launched five years ago. manchester ink link reported that 533 students across new hampshire received the distinction this year. because some demonstrated proficiency in more than one additional language, the state issued 547 awards. languages represented included spanish, french, portuguese, arabic, ukrainian, vietnamese, chinese and american sign language, among many others. the seal recognizes graduating students who meet english requirements and demonstrate intermediate-level proficiency in listening, speaking, reading and writing in another language. approved assessments include advanced placement, international baccalaureate and other state-recognized language tests. recipients receive a seal on their diploma, a state certificate and a graduation cord. the manchester group shows how the recognition is reaching students in the state’s largest school district. state education officials describe multilingual ability as useful for community connections and future work. new hampshire also recognized 48 middle-school students with a junior seal of biliteracy, extending the program’s pathway to younger learners. new-hampshire new-hampshire new hampshire nh manchester manchester, nh new hampshire manchester education languages
